extracted.intended_audience: recipients of education programs and activities (K–12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, and institutional compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and implementation guidance for §106.44 (emergency removal, partial removals, administrative leave) and §106.44(j) (prohibited disclosures of personally identifiable information) in the Department's final Title IX regulations. Focused on when and how institutions may remove individuals or disclose information while protecting due process and other statutory rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal substantive standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency removal is permitted where, after an individualized assessment, the respondent poses an 'imminent and serious threat to individual safety' in the recipient's education program or activity; this can include threats beyond physical violence and may include non-physical threats to health or safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that emergency removal may be justified for threats that are not strictly physical (e.g., verbal sexual harassment that produces a serious threat); the standard confirms that mere strongly articulated viewpoints—even if offensive—do not meet the threshold. The Department notes the 2020 amendments recognized emergency removal for threats of violence and that 'threats beyond acts of physical violence may justify emergency removal.' Recipients must apply an individualized assessment to balance the need to protect safety with preventing misuse to bypass grievance procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal procedural safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient effectuates an emergency removal under §106.44(h), it must afford the respondent notice and an opportunity to challenge the removal 'immediately following the removal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post-removal notice and prompt opportunity to challenge are required to protect due process. The preamble notes recipients commonly 'accommodate students who have been removed on an emergency basis with alternative means to continue academic coursework during a removal period' and that the post-removal process provides an opportunity to raise concerns about continued access to coursework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of emergency removal — partial removals permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient has discretion to remove a respondent on an emergency basis from 'all or part' of its education program or activity (e.g., particular classes, teams, clubs, organizations, or activities) provided the requirements of §106.44(h) are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial emergency removal may be sufficient when it addresses an imminent and serious safety risk and can reduce burdens on the respondent. The Department affirms discretion to narrow removals where appropriate and references 85 FR 30232 for examples. The option to narrow removal does not relieve the recipient of meeting the substantive and procedural requirements for emergency removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between supportive measures and emergency removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial removal may alternatively be implemented as a supportive measure under §106.44(g) rather than as an emergency removal under §106.44(h); whether an action is a supportive measure or an emergency removal depends on meeting the respective provision's requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures must be consistent with §106.44(g) and the definition of supportive measures in §106.2; they must not unreasonably burden a party (§106.44(g)(2)). If implemented as a supportive measure, different procedural protections apply than under emergency removal (which requires immediate post-removal notice and opportunity to challenge). Administrative leave may be used either as a supportive measure or under emergency removal procedures when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment considerations for emergency removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX enforcement and the emergency removal provisions must be applied 'consistent with the requirements of the First Amendment'; protected expression—even if offensive—does not by itself justify emergency removal unless it meets the serious/imminent threat standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department states it is 'unaware of circumstances in which such speech has been the basis for removal under the lower standard' and declines to amend §106.44(h) based on commenters' concerns that speech could be subject to emergency removal. Recipients must avoid restricting rights otherwise protected from government action by the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of emergency removal with other federal laws (IDEA, Section 504, ADA, FERPA, Clery Act, Title VII/VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(h) does not modify or override rights under IDEA, Section 504, the ADA, FERPA, the Clery Act, Title VI, or Title VII; recipients must ensure compliance with those laws when implementing emergency removal or related actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may need to treat students with disabilities differently (e.g., manifestation determination review under IDEA in some cases) and may involve the student's IEP or Section 504 team before removal. Disclosures required by FERPA or the Clery Act generally remain permitted under §106.44(j). The Department clarifies that while procedures for other statutes may differ, Title IX's emergency removal requirements are appropriate for addressing sex discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal not admissible as 'relevant evidence' under §106.45 determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: An emergency removal is not 'relevant evidence' that can be considered in reaching a determination under §106.45(b)(6) and (h)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarifies that emergency removal decisions should not influence the outcome of grievance determinations of responsibility, which preserves the presumption of non-responsibility and prevents circumvention of procedural protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative leave for employee respondents — scope and discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.44(i), recipients may place employee respondents (including student employees) on administrative leave during the pendency of grievance procedures; this is discretionary, generally temporary, and understood as a separation from employment usually with pay and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes administrative leave does not presume responsibility and that disciplinary sanctions require compliance with §106.45 (and §106.46 if applicable) before imposition. Administrative leave used as a supportive measure must comply with §106.44(g) (including not unreasonably burdening a party and generally being paid). Recipients must also respect State laws, collective bargaining agreements, and employment contracts; §106.44(i) does not override those obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative leave applicability to non-employee individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Although §106.44(i) is understood to apply to employees, recipients may determine—consistent with state law and institutional policies—whether volunteers, agents, or others authorized to provide aid, benefits, or services are treated as employees for purposes of administrative leave, and may remove such non-employees via supportive measures or emergency removal when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to expand §106.44(i) explicitly to volunteers/agents, noting variance in employment arrangements across states; however, recipients may follow their own policies regarding non-employees provided those policies comply with Title IX and other applicable law. §106.44(i) does not prevent removing non-employees as a supportive measure or on an emergency basis per §106.44(g)/(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disclosure of personally identifiable information (PII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j) protects 'all personally identifiable information obtained by a recipient in the course of complying with the Department's Title IX regulations' from disclosure, subject to specified exceptions, to prevent chilling reporting and participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department adopted the broader term 'personally identifiable information' (information that would tend to reveal the identity of an individual) rather than just 'identity' to protect sensitive data including information about pregnancy or related conditions, sexual orientation, gender identity, or other sex characteristics. The preamble explains nondisclosure is necessary to avoid chilling effects and to protect against retaliation, harassment, or other sex-based harm. Disclosures that are otherwise permitted under other federal statutes/regulations (e.g., FERPA, Clery Act) are discussed as exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to the PII nondisclosure rule (existence and example)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(j) contains five exceptions to the general prohibition on disclosure of PII; one example is disclosure with prior written consent from 'a person with the legal right to consent to the disclosure' (read consistently with FERPA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent must come from the person with legal authority under applicable law (e.g., a parent/guardian for a minor in K–12 when FERPA applies). Even where an exception applies, disclosures cannot be made for retaliatory purposes per §106.71. Commenters requested additional exceptions (e.g., disclosures required by federal grant terms), and the Department considered interactions with FERPA and HIPAA when defining the scope and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad application of PII protections across Title IX contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: The PII nondisclosure protection applies to personally identifiable information obtained in any Title IX-related context (informal resolution, grievance procedures, supportive measures, remedies, reasonable modifications), not only the narrow contexts enumerated in the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised the regulation so PII protections cover situations like reasonable modifications for pregnancy or related conditions, recognizing that privacy interests are the same regardless of whether a formal complaint exists. The protection is intended to ensure individuals (or parents/guardians of minors) have a reasonable expectation that PII shared in Title IX contexts 'generally will not be disclosed to third parties.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to consult IEP/Section 504 teams for students with disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve rights of students with disabilities, final regulations include §106.8(e), which requires a recipient's Title IX Coordinator or designee to consult with appropriate members of a student's IEP or Section 504 team when complying with §106.45.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes that §106.44(h) does not modify IDEA or Section 504 rights and that recipients might need to treat respondent students with disabilities differently (e.g., involve the IEP/504 team, consider manifestation determinations) before making emergency removal decisions. The consultation requirement helps ensure compliance with disability-specific procedural protections.
